question: Why do you want to study Strength and Conditioning?
lookingFor: Genuine motivation rooted in real exposure to training, not just a love of sport or the gym.

bullets: Point to a concrete experience that sparked the interest, not a vague love of fitness
Show you understand S&C is a science and coaching discipline, not just lifting weights
Connect the motivation to what you want to do with it long term
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I got properly interested when I tore my hamstring at sixteen and the physio who rebuilt my sprinting used a return-to-play program that was basically applied strength and conditioning. Watching how deliberately he built load back up, week by week, made me realise this was a real science with a huge amount of decision making behind it, not just telling someone to lift more. I started reading about periodization after that and ended up helping coach the school athletics squad's off season program. I want to study it properly because I want to be the person making those calls for athletes one day, not just following a plan someone else wrote.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I love the gym' with nothing else behind it
Talking only about their own training with no coaching angle
Confusing S&C with personal training or bodybuilding
followUps: What part of that experience specifically made you want to coach rather than just train yourself?

question: Why did you choose our Strength and Conditioning course over other sport science degrees?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to this course's structure, not generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific feature: placement structure, accreditation, lab facilities, a named module or staff member
Explain why that feature matters to their own goals
Show they understand how this differs from a general sports science degree
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Most sports science degrees I looked at treat strength and conditioning as one module among many, but yours builds the whole degree around it and is accredited toward the UKSCA, which matters to me because I want to be coaching professionally within a few years of graduating. The placement in second year with a professional club's performance staff was the deciding factor, since I want hands on experience with athlete monitoring, not just lecture theory. I also read about the biomechanics lab work students do on lifting technique, which is exactly the kind of applied detail I want to get good at.

commonMistakes: Praise that could apply to any university
Not distinguishing S&C from general sport science or exercise physiology
Leading with rankings rather than course content
followUps: What would you want to get out of that placement specifically?

question: What first got you interested in strength and conditioning as opposed to just playing sport?
lookingFor: A clear moment or realisation that shows the shift from participant to someone curious about the training process itself.

bullets: Describe a specific turning point, not a gradual and vague interest
Show curiosity about the how and why behind training, not just results
Link it to taking initiative, such as reading or shadowing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I was a decent club level rower but plateaued for almost a year, and it was only when our coach brought in a strength and conditioning specialist to redesign our winter program that my times actually moved again. What struck me was that he could explain exactly why each block was structured the way it was, tied to our race demands, rather than just handing out a generic gym sheet. That was the moment I stopped caring about my own numbers and started wanting to understand the reasoning behind everyone's program.

commonMistakes: Just saying they always loved sport
No specific moment or example
Framing it entirely around their own performance with no coaching curiosity
followUps: Did you ever ask that coach directly about his reasoning, and what did you learn?

question: Tell us about any experience you have coaching, training, or working with athletes.
lookingFor: Concrete, specific experience with genuine reflection on what was learned, even if informal.

bullets: Give specifics: who, what age or level, what the role actually involved
Reflect on a real decision or problem they had to work through
Be honest about the scale of the experience rather than overselling it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been assistant coaching my old school's under fifteen rugby strength sessions for the past year, working under a qualified coach who lets me plan the warm ups and run the movement prep. The hardest thing I've had to figure out is how much to individualise within a group of fifteen boys who are at wildly different training ages, since a couple of them had never touched a barbell. I ended up running two simplified tracks within the same session so everyone was progressing safely, which taught me a lot about the gap between an ideal program and what's actually deliverable with limited time and equipment.

commonMistakes: Overstating informal experience as if it were professional coaching
Listing activities with no reflection on what was learned
Having genuinely no exposure and not being honest about it
followUps: How did you decide what to prioritise for the less experienced boys?

question: What have you read or followed outside of school that's shaped your understanding of strength and conditioning?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine, ongoing engagement with the field beyond the curriculum, with some critical thinking about it.

bullets: Name specific sources: a book, a journal, a coach or podcast, not just 'the internet'
Explain a specific idea taken from it, not just that it was read
Show some critical engagement rather than treating it as gospel
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Mike Israetel's writing on training volume and recovery, and more recently worked through parts of Bompa's periodization textbook, which was a lot denser but genuinely useful for understanding how macrocycles get built. What struck me was how much disagreement there still is in the field, for instance around how much velocity based training actually adds over simpler RPE methods, and I like that it's not a solved science. I also follow the NSCA's published research summaries to try to separate what's actually evidence backed from what's just popular on social media.

commonMistakes: Naming only social media influencers with no critical distance
Vague claims of reading 'a lot' with no specifics
Treating everything read as settled fact rather than an evolving field
followUps: Where did you disagree with something you read, and why?

question: How would you explain the difference between a strength and conditioning coach and a personal trainer?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate distinction showing they understand the profession they're applying to study, not just gym culture.

bullets: Focus on population: athletes and sport performance versus general fitness clients
Mention the emphasis on performance outcomes tied to a sport, not aesthetics or general health alone
Note the team context, working alongside coaches, physios and sport scientists
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A personal trainer usually works one to one with general clients on goals like fat loss or general fitness, whereas a strength and conditioning coach designs training specifically to improve performance in a sport, so everything gets built around the physical demands of that sport and often around a whole squad rather than one person. An S&C coach also typically sits within a wider performance team, working alongside physios, sport scientists and the head coach, so a lot of the job is communication and fitting training around a competition calendar, not just writing a good program in isolation.

commonMistakes: Saying they're basically the same job
Focusing only on qualifications rather than the actual role
Ignoring the team and periodization context entirely
followUps: Why does that team context matter for how a program actually gets designed?

question: Can you explain the principle of progressive overload?
lookingFor: A clear, correct explanation of the concept with a real example of how it's applied.

bullets: State that the body adapts only when demand is gradually increased over time
Mention the variables that can be manipulated: load, volume, frequency, or difficulty
Give a concrete example of applying it safely
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Progressive overload is the idea that the body only keeps adapting if the training demand keeps increasing gradually, because if you repeat the exact same stimulus your body has no reason to keep changing. That doesn't just mean adding weight, it can mean increasing reps, sets, frequency, or reducing rest, and a good coach picks whichever variable makes sense for where the athlete is. For example, with a beginner I'd rather add a small amount of weight each week on a squat once technique is solid, rather than jumping load too fast and risking form breaking down.

commonMistakes: Saying it just means adding weight every session with no nuance
Ignoring the risk of overloading too fast
No concrete example given
followUps: What would make you choose to increase volume rather than load for a given athlete?

question: What is periodization and why is it important in a training program?
lookingFor: A working understanding of structuring training across time toward a competition goal, with correct terminology.

bullets: Define periodization as structured variation of training over time toward a specific goal or competition
Mention the general structure: macrocycle, mesocycle, microcycle, or phases like general prep to peaking
Explain why it matters: managing fatigue, avoiding plateaus or overtraining, peaking at the right time
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Periodization is planning training in structured phases over weeks and months rather than repeating the same session indefinitely, usually broken into a macrocycle for the whole year, mesocycles of a few weeks focused on a particular quality, and microcycles which are the individual weeks. It matters because an athlete can't be at peak fatigue and peak freshness at the same time, so you have to sequence building work like hypertrophy or general strength earlier, then shift toward power and speed closer to competition. Without that structure you risk either undertraining because nothing progresses, or overtraining because fatigue never gets managed down before it matters most.

commonMistakes: Confusing periodization with just having a training plan
No mention of managing fatigue versus peaking
Using the terms macrocycle and microcycle incorrectly or interchangeably
followUps: How might periodization for a team sport athlete differ from an individual athlete with one big competition?

question: What does the principle of specificity mean, and can you give an example of it going wrong?
lookingFor: Understanding that adaptations are specific to the demands placed on the body, plus awareness of common misapplications.

bullets: Explain that training adaptations closely match the type of stress applied
Give a real or plausible example of specificity being respected or ignored
Show awareness that specificity has to be balanced against building a general base
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Specificity means the body adapts closely to the exact type of demand you train, so if you want to get faster you need to actually train speed, not just get generally fitter and hope it transfers. A classic example of it going wrong is a distance runner doing long slow steady state cardio thinking it will help a five kilometre race pace, when in reality they need work closer to actual race intensity to see real improvement there. That said, I think specificity has to be balanced against a general base early on, especially with younger or less trained athletes, because going too specific too soon can leave gaps that limit them later.

commonMistakes: Confusing specificity with simply doing the sport itself as training
No example given, purely definitional answer
Ignoring the need for a general base before specialising
followUps: At what stage of an athlete's development would you start prioritising more sport-specific work?

question: Briefly explain the difference between aerobic and anaerobic energy systems and why it matters for programming.
lookingFor: Correct basic physiology plus an understanding of why it shapes how conditioning is designed for different sports.

bullets: Aerobic system uses oxygen for sustained lower intensity effort, anaerobic systems fuel short intense efforts without oxygen
Mention that most sports use a blend, not purely one or the other
Connect it to programming: matching conditioning work to the sport's actual energy demands
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The aerobic system uses oxygen to produce energy and is what powers longer, lower intensity efforts, while the anaerobic systems, the phosphocreatine and glycolytic pathways, fuel short bursts of high intensity work without needing oxygen but fatigue much faster. Almost no sport sits purely in one system, a football match for example is mostly aerobic but decided by repeated anaerobic sprints and tackles, so conditioning has to reflect that blend rather than just building a big aerobic base. Getting that balance wrong, like over-emphasising steady state running for a sport that's actually stop start, means the conditioning doesn't transfer to what actually happens in the game.

commonMistakes: Treating a sport as purely one energy system
Confusing the phosphocreatine and glycolytic anaerobic pathways
No connection made to actual programming decisions
followUps: How would you design conditioning differently for a sprinter versus a marathon runner?

question: How does an S&C coach typically work alongside physiotherapists and sport coaches, and why does that relationship matter?
lookingFor: Understanding that S&C sits within a collaborative, communication-heavy team rather than working in isolation.

bullets: Recognise S&C is rarely independent, it depends on constant communication with medical and coaching staff
Give an example of where miscommunication could cause harm, such as return to play
Show understanding that priorities can conflict and need negotiating, like fatigue management versus tactical demands
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An S&C coach has to work closely with physios especially around injury and return to play, because loading an athlete back up too fast without checking in constantly can undo the rehab work entirely, and closely with the head coach because tactical priorities and competition schedule dictate how much fatigue an athlete can actually absorb that week. I think the relationship matters most when priorities clash, for example a coach wanting more pitch time right before a big game while the S&C coach can see fatigue markers creeping up, and navigating that disagreement well without just deferring or digging in is a real skill. It's as much a communication job as a technical one.

commonMistakes: Describing S&C as an independent role with no collaboration
No example of conflicting priorities or how to navigate them
Ignoring the medical side entirely and focusing only on coaches
followUps: What would you do if a head coach wanted an athlete to train through what you thought was excessive fatigue?

subtopic: Designing a program for a beginner
question: If you were asked to design a basic strength program for a young athlete who had never trained before, what would you prioritise?
lookingFor: Sensible, safety-first thinking that shows understanding of training age and long-term development, not just enthusiasm for heavy lifting.

bullets: Prioritise technique and movement competency before load
Mention appropriate volume and simplicity given low training age
Reference long term athletic development and making training enjoyable and sustainable
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start with movement quality rather than load, teaching fundamental patterns like a squat, hinge, push and pull with just bodyweight or very light resistance until technique is genuinely solid, since a young athlete's training age means the biggest early gains come from motor learning, not heavy weight. I'd keep the program simple, maybe two or three sessions a week with a handful of exercises done well rather than a complicated split, and build in enough variety that it stays enjoyable so they actually want to keep coming back. Long term I'd be thinking about their athletic development over years, not trying to maximise strength in the first few months.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to load and intensity for a total beginner
Overcomplicating the program with too many exercises
No mention of long-term development or enjoyment, purely short-term output
followUps: How would you know when they're ready to progress from bodyweight to loaded movements?

question: What role can strength and conditioning play in preventing injuries?
lookingFor: Understanding that S&C reduces injury risk through targeted, evidence-informed work, while being careful not to overclaim it eliminates injury.

bullets: Mention building tissue capacity and resilience through progressive loading
Give a concrete example, like eccentric hamstring work reducing strain injuries
Be honest that S&C reduces risk rather than guarantees prevention, since injury is multifactorial
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Strength and conditioning helps reduce injury risk by building tissue capacity gradually so muscles, tendons and joints can tolerate the actual demands of the sport, and there's good evidence for specific interventions, like eccentric hamstring work such as Nordic curls reducing hamstring strain rates in sports with a lot of sprinting. I'd be careful to say it reduces risk rather than prevents injury outright, because injury is multifactorial and things like fixture congestion or contact incidents are largely outside a coach's control. What I find interesting is that a lot of the job is really about managing acute spikes in load, since a sudden jump in training or match demand is one of the strongest predictors of injury.

commonMistakes: Claiming S&C can eliminate injury entirely
No concrete example of an evidence-based intervention
Ignoring load management and acute-to-chronic workload considerations
followUps: What would you look for as a warning sign that an athlete's load has increased too quickly?

question: What is RPE and how might a coach use it to adjust training?
lookingFor: Correct definition of rate of perceived exertion plus practical understanding of autoregulation.

bullets: Define RPE as a subjective scale of how hard an effort felt, often out of ten
Explain autoregulation: adjusting load or volume session to session based on reported effort
Note its limitations, such as reliance on athlete honesty and experience reading their own body
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: RPE, rate of perceived exertion, is a subjective scale, usually out of ten, where an athlete rates how hard a set or session actually felt, which is often paired with reps in reserve to estimate how many more reps they could have done. Coaches use it for autoregulation, so instead of a fixed number on the bar every week, the load gets adjusted day to day based on how the athlete is actually responding, which accounts for things like poor sleep or accumulated fatigue that a rigid plan can't see. The main limitation is it depends on the athlete being honest and having enough experience to rate effort accurately, so it tends to work better with more trained athletes than complete beginners.

commonMistakes: Confusing RPE with heart rate or an objective measure
No mention of its subjective limitations
Not connecting it to actual program adjustment
followUps: Why might RPE be less reliable with a very inexperienced lifter?

question: Why is recovery just as important as the training itself?
lookingFor: Understanding that adaptation happens during recovery, not the workout, with awareness of overtraining risk.

bullets: Explain that training creates the stimulus but adaptation happens during rest and recovery
Mention sleep and nutrition as central, not just rest days
Note the risk of overtraining or non-functional overreaching without adequate recovery
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Training is really just the stimulus that signals the body to adapt, but the actual adaptation, whether that's muscle repair or the nervous system getting more efficient, happens during recovery, so a hard session without enough sleep and nutrition afterward is a wasted opportunity. Sleep in particular gets underrated, since that's when most of the hormonal environment for repair and growth is most favourable. If recovery is consistently insufficient, athletes can slide into overtraining or non-functional overreaching, where performance actually declines and the risk of injury and illness goes up, so respecting recovery isn't optional, it's part of the program.

commonMistakes: Treating recovery as an afterthought rather than part of the program
Only mentioning rest days and ignoring sleep or nutrition
No awareness of overtraining as a real risk
followUps: What signs might tell a coach an athlete isn't recovering adequately between sessions?

question: There's a common belief that lifting weights stunts a child's growth. How would you respond to a worried parent?
lookingFor: Evidence-based reassurance delivered with tact, showing they can communicate science to a non-expert audience.

bullets: State clearly that current evidence does not support weight training stunting growth when properly supervised
Acknowledge the real risk is poor technique or excessive load, not weight training itself
Show empathy for the parent's concern rather than dismissing it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start by acknowledging the concern is understandable, since it's a widely repeated myth, but explain that the research, including position statements from bodies like the NSCA, doesn't support properly supervised resistance training stunting growth or damaging growth plates. The actual risk comes from poor technique, excessive load too soon, or inadequate supervision, not from resistance training itself, which is why a good program for a young athlete emphasises movement quality and appropriate progression rather than maximal loads. I'd rather walk the parent through exactly what a session would look like than just quote a study at them, because trust matters more than being technically right.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the parent's concern as ignorant rather than addressing it
Getting the science wrong or overstating certainty
No mention of what actually does create risk for young athletes
followUps: What specific safeguards would you put in place for a group of young athletes new to the weight room?

question: An athlete you're working with asks your opinion on performance enhancing drugs because a teammate is using them and seeing faster results. What would you say?
lookingFor: Clear ethical position combined with a constructive, non-judgemental response that keeps the athlete engaged rather than shutting the conversation down.

bullets: Be unambiguous that using banned substances is not something they'd support or facilitate
Address the underlying frustration or impatience driving the question, not just the rule
Show they'd keep the conversation open rather than reacting with judgement that shuts the athlete down
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd be honest and clear that I wouldn't support using banned substances, both because it's against the rules of their sport and because the long-term health risks are real and often understated. But I wouldn't just leave it there, because the question usually comes from genuine frustration at slower progress, so I'd want to understand what's actually driving it and check whether their current program and recovery are actually optimised, since there's often more room for legitimate progress than people realise. I'd rather keep that conversation open and be someone they can be honest with than react in a way that makes them stop asking me things.

commonMistakes: Giving a wishy-washy answer that avoids taking a clear position
Reacting with pure judgement in a way that would shut the athlete down
Ignoring the underlying motivation behind the question
followUps: What would you do if you suspected an athlete was already using something without admitting it?

question: Why can't the same training program work equally well for every athlete on a team?
lookingFor: Understanding of individual differences: training age, injury history, anthropometry, and psychological response to training.

bullets: Mention training age and experience level differing widely even within one squad
Reference injury history and individual movement limitations
Note that response to training volume and stress also varies psychologically, not just physically
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Even within one team, athletes can have wildly different training ages, so a program that's appropriately challenging for someone who's lifted for five years might be dangerous for someone who started three months ago. Injury history matters too, an athlete coming back from an ACL reconstruction needs very different loading around the knee than someone with no history at all. And it's not just physical, some athletes thrive on high volume and others burn out or lose motivation under the same load, so part of individualising is paying attention to how someone's responding psychologically, not just what the spreadsheet says they should be lifting.

commonMistakes: Only mentioning physical differences and ignoring training age or history
Treating individualisation as impossible at team scale, offering no practical solution
No acknowledgement of psychological response to training
followUps: How would you practically individualise a program for a squad of twenty without writing twenty separate plans?

question: What do you think about the growing use of wearable technology and GPS data in strength and conditioning?
lookingFor: Balanced view that recognises the value of data while being wary of over-reliance on technology over coaching judgement.

bullets: Acknowledge the genuine benefit: objective load tracking and earlier detection of fatigue or risk
Raise a real limitation, such as data overload or coaches losing feel for the athlete in front of them
Land on technology as a tool that supports, not replaces, coaching judgement
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it's genuinely useful, GPS data on distance covered and high speed running lets a coach see workload trends that would be impossible to judge by eye, and that objectivity has clearly helped reduce soft tissue injuries in sports that have adopted it well. My concern is that it's easy to generate more data than anyone can meaningfully act on, and I've read about teams drowning in metrics without a clear framework for what actually changes a decision. I see it as something that should sharpen a coach's judgement, not replace the conversation with the athlete about how they're actually feeling that day.

commonMistakes: Treating technology as either useless or as a complete replacement for coaching judgement
No awareness of data overload as a real problem
Vague answer with no specific example of a metric or use case
followUps: If the data and the athlete's own reported feeling disagreed, which would you trust more, and why?

question: Pick a lift you know well and explain what you'd check to make sure the technique is safe and effective.
lookingFor: Applied biomechanical knowledge grounded in an example, not just memorised cues.

bullets: Choose a specific lift and describe two or three concrete technical checkpoints
Connect the checkpoint to why it matters, injury risk or force production, not just 'that's the cue'
Show they understand technique can vary reasonably between individuals, not one rigid template
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'll take the deadlift, since it's the one I've spent the most time coaching younger athletes on. I'd check the bar stays close to the shins throughout the pull, because as soon as it drifts forward the load moves further from the hips and lower back and the spine takes more strain to compensate. I'd also watch that the hips and shoulders rise together rather than the hips shooting up first, which usually means someone's turning it into more of a stiff legged movement and losing hamstring involvement. I'd keep in mind that stance width and bar position can reasonably differ between individuals based on limb length, so I'm not chasing one identical picture for every athlete, just those underlying principles.

commonMistakes: Listing cues without explaining the biomechanical reason behind them
Picking a lift they clearly don't know well
Treating technique as one rigid universal template with no individual variation
followUps: How would you adapt that lift for an athlete with notably long legs relative to their torso?

question: How might the amount of feedback a coach gives affect how well an athlete learns a new lifting technique?
lookingFor: Some awareness that motor learning research suggests too much feedback can actually hinder retention, showing depth beyond basic coaching cues.

bullets: Recognise that constant correction can create dependency rather than genuine learning
Reference the idea of allowing self-correction or reduced feedback frequency to build internal awareness
Balance this against the real need for correction with beginners or safety-critical errors
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: From what I've read on motor learning, giving feedback after every single rep can actually slow down real learning, because the athlete starts relying on the coach's voice instead of building their own sense of what the movement should feel like. Some research suggests reducing feedback frequency, or letting the athlete try to self-correct first before stepping in, builds better long-term retention than constant correction. That said, I wouldn't apply that blindly with a total beginner or if there's a genuine safety risk in the technique, where I think more frequent, direct correction is worth the trade-off early on.

commonMistakes: Assuming more feedback is always better with no nuance
No awareness of self-correction or feedback frequency as a real concept
Overapplying reduced feedback even in unsafe beginner situations
followUps: How would you tell the difference between an athlete who needs more feedback and one who needs less?

question: Some people argue free weights are always superior to machines for athletes. Do you agree?
lookingFor: Ability to hold a nuanced, evidence-aware position rather than repeating gym culture dogma.

bullets: Acknowledge free weights' advantage in stability demand and movement transfer for many sports
Give a legitimate case for machines: isolating a muscle, managing injury, beginners learning load tolerance safely
Land on the answer depending on the athlete and goal rather than a blanket rule
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't fully agree, though I understand where the argument comes from, since free weights demand stability and coordination that often transfers better to sport. But machines have real advantages too, for example isolating a specific muscle during rehab when you need to load a joint in a very controlled way, or letting a total beginner build confidence and tolerance to load before they've got the coordination for a barbell movement safely. I think the honest answer is it depends on the athlete and the goal at that point in their development, and a good coach uses both rather than being dogmatic about it.

commonMistakes: Taking an absolute position with no nuance either way
No concrete example of when machines are genuinely useful
Dismissing the question instead of engaging with the actual trade-offs
followUps: Can you think of a specific athlete or situation where you'd choose a machine over a free weight version of the same movement?

question: Tell us about a time you designed or adjusted a training plan for yourself or someone else based on something you'd learned.
lookingFor: A real, specific example showing they can move from theory to practice and reflect on the outcome.

bullets: Describe a specific, real situation, not a hypothetical
Show the reasoning: what was learned and why it changed the approach
Reflect honestly on what happened, including if it didn't fully work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: After reading about undulating periodization, I rewrote my own off-season training block to vary intensity and volume day to day instead of sticking with the same rep ranges every session like I had been. I was curious whether it would actually feel different, and within about six weeks I noticed I was recovering better between heavy sessions and my squat numbers moved more than they had in the previous block using a more linear approach. It wasn't a perfectly controlled comparison since a lot else changes over six weeks too, but it made me genuinely appreciate why coaches choose one periodization model over another rather than it just being textbook theory.

commonMistakes: Giving a hypothetical rather than a real example
No reasoning connecting the theory learned to the decision made
Overclaiming certainty about results without acknowledging confounding factors
followUps: What would you want to control for if you tried to test that more rigorously?

question: How would you handle an athlete who keeps skipping their gym sessions even though you know it's holding back their performance?
lookingFor: A coaching-minded, empathetic approach that seeks to understand the cause before jumping to enforcement.

bullets: Prioritise understanding the underlying reason before assuming laziness or lack of care
Consider practical barriers, such as session length, timing, or the program feeling irrelevant to them
Show willingness to adjust the approach rather than just repeating instructions louder
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first instinct wouldn't be to assume they don't care, I'd want to sit down and actually ask what's going on, because it's often something practical like the session clashing with something else in their life, or the program feeling disconnected from what they actually care about improving in their sport. If it turned out the sessions felt boring or irrelevant to them, I'd look at making the program more clearly tied to specific things they've told me they want to get better at, since buy-in tends to follow relevance. I'd rather adjust my approach a couple of times than just keep repeating the same instruction and hoping it eventually lands.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to discipline or blame without investigating the cause
Assuming it's purely a motivation problem rather than a practical or program design issue
Offering no willingness to adapt their own coaching approach
followUps: What would you do if you found out the real reason was something outside training entirely, like a personal issue?

question: Where do you see the field of strength and conditioning heading in the next decade?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with current trends in the profession, showing the applicant follows the field rather than just the practice of it.

bullets: Name a specific real trend, such as data driven individualisation, or growth in youth and women's sport specific research
Give a reasoned opinion on it rather than just listing buzzwords
Show awareness that increased data still needs a skilled coach to interpret it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think one of the biggest shifts is the amount of research finally being done specifically on female athletes, who were historically underrepresented in sport science studies, and that's already starting to change things like how training gets adjusted around the menstrual cycle. I also expect individualisation to keep growing as monitoring technology gets cheaper and more accessible even outside elite sport, so programs stop being written for an 'average' athlete. My worry is that the technology gets ahead of coaches' ability to interpret it well, so I think the coaches who actually understand the underlying physiology behind the data will be the ones who benefit most, not just whoever has the fanciest equipment.

commonMistakes: Vague buzzwords like 'technology' with no specific trend named
No personal opinion or reasoning, just a list
Assuming more data automatically means better coaching with no caveat
followUps: Which of those trends are you personally most excited to work with, and why?
